strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely question: how to fuse the complementary strengths of vision-only foundation models (DINOv2) and vision-language models (CLIP) for transductive zero-shot learning without any additional training.

The proposed OTFusion formulation is conceptually simple, casting distribution fusion as an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem solved via Sinkhorn iterations, and is compatible with multiple VFMs/VLMs in principle.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 11 standard ZSL benchmarks and two backbones (CLIP ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50), with comparisons to numerous recent training-based and training-free baselines (TPT, DiffTPT, CoCoOp, TDA, DMN, TransCLIP, ECALP, etc.).

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of the semantic-only, visual-only, concatenation, and joint-learning components, plus sensitivity analyses for the entropy and fusion hyperparameters and a convergence study.

Reported average gains over the CLIP baseline (~10%) and improvements over several strong recent transductive baselines (e.g., TransCLIP, ECALP) on most datasets are substantial, suggesting practical value if the comparisons are fair.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior transductive CLIP adaptation via GMM + optimal transport (TransCLIP, Zanella et al. 2024), which already models a shared-covariance GMM visual prior and OT-based fusion; the main new ingredient is substituting/adding a DINOv2 visual prior, which is a relatively small conceptual step despite being framed as a fully novel perspective and method.

The claim of being 'the first work that systematically investigates the complementary strengths of VFMs and VLMs' is overstated given that Imam et al. 2024 already explores exactly this combination (albeit via training-based prompt tuning); the distinction should be more precisely scoped to 'training-free'.

There are notational inconsistencies and apparent errors in the optimal transport formulation: the same symbol K is overloaded for the number of foundation models, the number of classes, and the Sinkhorn kernel matrix; the doubly stochastic constraint as written (Q1_K = 1_N, Q^T1_N = 1_K) is dimensionally inconsistent with typical class-imbalanced marginals (it implicitly requires N = K unless properly normalized), which undermines confidence in the precision of the derivation as presented.

The comparison may not be entirely apples-to-apples: OTFusion additionally requires a full forward pass of a large DINOv2 ViT-L/14 model over the entire test set, which is a nontrivial extra inference cost not discussed or quantified against training-free baselines that use only the CLIP encoder; no wall-clock/runtime comparison is provided despite claims of being 'lightweight' and 'scalable'.

The CLIP baseline uses a single fixed prompt template without ensembling, which may be weaker than the prompt-ensembled CLIP baselines commonly reported in the literature and used by some comparison methods; this could inflate the reported percentage improvement over 'the original CLIP model' without necessarily reflecting the same relative gain over stronger CLIP baselines.

The generalization of the framework to multiple VLMs (not just multiple VFMs) is asserted (Eq. 6, Extension section) but never empirically validated in the experiments, leaving an important scalability claim unverified.

No variance/robustness analysis (e.g., multiple runs, sensitivity to GMM initialization or random seeds) is reported, which is relevant since GMM-based clustering can be sensitive to initialization even with the proposed VLM-guided init.
Minor numerical inconsistencies exist between tables (e.g., CLIP ImageNet accuracy reported as 66.73 in Table 1 vs. 66.60 in Table 2), suggesting some lack of care in result reporting.

strengths: The core motivation—leveraging complementary strengths of self-supervised VFMs (strong visual clustering) and VLMs (semantic alignment) for transductive ZSL—is well-articulated and supported by an intuitive t-SNE visualization.

The proposed OT-based fusion formulation (entropy-regularized transport coupling GMM-derived visual posteriors and VLM semantic posteriors, solved via Sinkhorn) is clean, training-free, and computationally lightweight compared to prompt-tuning alternatives.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 11 standard benchmarks with two backbones (CLIP ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50), showing consistent and often large improvements over CLIP and several strong baselines (TDA, DMN, TransCLIP, ECALP).

Reasonably thorough ablation study isolating the role of each distribution source (Y-only, CLIP-only, DINOv2-only, concatenation, no joint-learning), which helps clarify which components drive the gains.
Sensitivity analysis on ϵ and λ, plus a convergence analysis, add some assurance about robustness and stability of the optimization procedure.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the underlying GMM/E-step + entropy-regularized transport machinery is largely inherited from TransCLIP (Zanella, Gerin, and Ayed 2024), with the main addition being substitution/fusion with a DINOv2-derived posterior. The paper would benefit from more precisely delineating what is new relative to this prior work rather than presenting the whole pipeline as a novel contribution.

The ablation results (Table 2) show that DINOv2-only already achieves 74.20% average accuracy, nearly matching the full OTFusion result of 74.95%, and CLIP-only alone at 70.96% versus full concatenation at 75.54% (which even beats OTFusion). This suggests the OT-based distribution fusion contributes marginally beyond simply having a strong DINOv2 visual prior, undermining the claimed importance of the OT fusion mechanism itself.

Despite the framework being motivated and formally extended (Eq. 6) to combine multiple VFMs and VLMs, the main experiments only ever use a single VFM (DINOv2) and single VLM (CLIP); the flexibility/scalability claims for multi-model fusion are not empirically substantiated.

The claimed compatibility with pseudo-label-based training methods (Lafter, CPL) mentioned in the introduction and abstract is never empirically demonstrated in the experimental section — no results show OTFusion enhancing these methods' pseudo-labels.

There are inconsistencies in reported baseline numbers: the CLIP baseline in Table 1(a) (average 64.78, with per-dataset values like ImageNet 66.73) differs from the 'native CLIP' baseline used in the ablation Table 2 (average 65.24, ImageNet 66.60), without any explanation of why these numbers differ (e.g., different prompt template or backbone variant).

The fixed λ = 0.8 used in the main experiments is inconsistent with the sensitivity analysis, which shows performance degrading for λ > 0.7 on several datasets (e.g., EuroSAT, Flowers102) — this discrepancy is not addressed or justified.

The extremely large accuracy gains on EuroSAT (+31–38%) are not analyzed in depth; given that EuroSAT is known to be sensitive to encoder choice and clustering structure, a deeper discussion of why gains are so much larger here versus other datasets (and whether this reflects real generalization benefit or dataset-specific quirks of DINOv2 features) is missing.

No computational cost/runtime comparison is provided against the compared training-free methods (TDA, DMN, TransCLIP, ECALP), despite claims of the method being 'lightweight' and 'scalable'; GMM fitting plus iterative Sinkhorn on large class counts (e.g., ImageNet with 1000 classes) could be non-trivial.
No variance/multiple-seed reporting is given for the results, which is relevant since GMM initialization and iterative refinement could introduce some run-to-run variability.
Code is not released with the submission (promised only post-acceptance), limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 26 datasets spanning three distinct domains (natural images, remote sensing, medical pathology), which is a notable breadth for a training-free method.

The core idea of casting multi-foundation-model fusion as a self-adaptive optimal transport problem is intuitive and practically appealing: it is training-free, prior-free, and does not require access to model weights, making it applicable to black-box/API-only models.

The self-adaptive weighting mechanism (via squared inner products) is given a principled optimization interpretation through an MM (Minorization-Maximization) derivation, with a convergence argument and empirical convergence curves showing fast convergence (~5-10 iterations).

Ablation studies are reasonably thorough, isolating the contributions of VFM introduction, self-adaptive weighting, and joint (vs. disjoint) GMM/OT learning, and a computational efficiency comparison (Table 6) situates the method favorably relative to graph-based transductive competitors.

Consistent and often substantial accuracy improvements over strong single-model and prior ensemble/transductive baselines (e.g., TransCLIP, ECALP, GTA-CLIP) are reported in both transductive and inductive settings.
weaknesses: Some reported gains over prior state-of-the-art methods (e.g., GTA-CLIP, TransCLIP) may partly stem from the extra information provided by additional strong VFMs (DINOv2/v3) rather than the fusion algorithm itself; the paper's own ablation (Only-P̂v vs. full SOTA) shows VLM-only ensembling yields much smaller gains, suggesting the headline numbers are not purely attributable to the proposed OT mechanism but to access to stronger auxiliary encoders, which complicates fair comparison with single-VLM baselines.

The central technical novelty—replacing the linear Frobenius inner product with its squared form to induce adaptive weights—is a fairly simple algebraic modification; while an MM-based optimization scheme is provided, there is limited theoretical justification for why this squared-term weighting reliably identifies model quality rather than reinforcing majority/overconfident predictions, beyond empirical validation.

The claim of being the 'first work to systematically investigate the complementary strengths of different foundation models' is an overclaim given the substantial prior literature on model ensembling and multi-view fusion, including OT-based fusion methods discussed in the related work section itself.

Key implementation details are underspecified or only partially justified: no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (ε, temperature τ, number of GMM components K), no discussion of how GMM covariance structure (diagonal vs. full) is chosen for high-dimensional CLIP/DINO features, and no error bars/variance across runs are reported.

The Gaussian Mixture Model assumption for VFM feature distributions is not well justified for high-dimensional deep features, and its fitting quality (especially with few samples in some datasets) is not analyzed.

The transductive setting requires access to the full test set to fit GMMs and solve OT jointly, which is a practical limitation for real-world deployment; the inductive variant mitigates this but at added complexity, and comparisons of computational/memory cost for the inductive setting are not clearly reported.

Some baseline comparisons (Tables 1-3) mix methods using single VLMs with SOTA variants using extra VFMs, making it difficult to disentangle the contribution of the proposed fusion algorithm from simply having access to more/better base models.

strengths: Well-motivated problem setting: the observation that VLMs over-rely on textual priors while VFMs provide complementary discriminative visual features (supported by Fig.1/Fig.6 clustering analyses) is clearly demonstrated and provides a solid empirical basis for the proposed fusion.

The self-adaptive optimal transport formulation is elegant and practically useful: replacing the linear Frobenius inner product with a squared term removes the need for manually tuned or validation-set-based model weights, which is important in the zero-shot setting where labels are unavailable.

Extensive empirical validation across 26 datasets spanning three very different domains (natural images, remote sensing, medical pathology) and both transductive/inductive settings, showing consistent and often substantial gains over strong recent baselines (TransCLIP, ECALP, GTA-CLIP, COSMIC, ADAPT, etc.).

Good supporting analyses: convergence curves (Fig.5), t-SNE visualizations (Fig.7), a principled MM-based optimization with convergence guarantees, computational/memory efficiency comparison (Table 6), and a model-subset ablation (Table 7) showing robustness to the specific combination of VLMs used.

Practical advantage of being training-free/prior-free and applicable to black-box (API-only) foundation models, which is appealing for real deployment scenarios where model weights are not accessible.
The ablations (VFM importance, self-adaptive vs fixed weighting, joint vs disjoint GMM/OT learning) are reasonably thorough and isolate the contribution of each design choice.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a combination of existing ingredients (entropic OT/Sinkhorn, GMM posterior estimation, MM optimization) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty largely lies in the specific squared-inner-product reweighting trick and its application to fusing VFMs+VLMs, which is somewhat incremental relative to prior transductive CLIP work (e.g., TransCLIP) that this paper builds directly upon.

The claim of being 'the first work to systematically investigate the complementary strengths of different foundation models in zero-shot classification' is strong and not fully substantiated against broader ensemble/multi-model fusion literature outside the specific OT framing; related ensembling ideas exist even if not framed via OT.

Some reported per-dataset results show negative deltas relative to individual baselines (e.g., Aircraft with CLIP-1+CLIP-2 in Table 1, -2.1), and the paper does not thoroughly discuss when/why the method can underperform a single strong model, beyond brief remarks in the ablation section.

The choice of GMM for modeling VFM feature distributions is a strong parametric assumption; its stability with limited samples per class (especially in the inductive/few-shot-like training regime) and sensitivity to initialization are not deeply analyzed.

No error bars, multiple random seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported, making it hard to assess whether some of the more modest gains (e.g., self-adaptive vs non-adaptive in Table 5) are robust.

The efficiency comparison (Table 6) provides Big-O complexity and wall-clock/memory numbers but does not clearly break down cost per component (GMM EM vs Sinkhorn iterations) or discuss scaling behavior as the number of models/classes grows substantially.

Minor presentation issues: some notational inconsistencies between the main text and appendix (e.g., Q_ic in Eq. 19 vs. T used elsewhere), and dense figures (e.g., Fig. 1, 2, 6) that are somewhat hard to parse quickly.
